claim: Detection of SARS-CoV-2 specific CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in SARS-CoV-2-unexposed donors has been explained by the presence of T cells primed by other coronaviruses.
source: Detection of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) specific CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in SARS-CoV-2-unexposed donors has been explained by the presence of T cells primed by other coronaviruses.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to existing literature in the introduction section discussing pre-existing SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells.

claim: Frequencies of SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells were higher in CMV-seropositive donors compared to CMV-seronegative donors.
source: Stimulation of pre-pandemic cryo-preserved peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) with SARS-CoV-2 peptides revealed that frequencies of SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells were higher in CMV-seropositive donors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from peptide stimulation assays shown in Figure 1.

claim: Membrane-specific CD4+ T cells originate from cross-reactive CMV-specific T cells.
source: Characterization of these T cells demonstrated that membrane-specific CD4+ and spike-specific CD8+ T cells originate from cross-reactive CMV-specific T cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing T cell clones reactive to both SARS-CoV-2 membrane and CMV pp65 peptides.

claim: Spike-specific CD8+ T cells originate from cross-reactive CMV-specific T cells.
source: Characterization of these T cells demonstrated that membrane-specific CD4+ and spike-specific CD8+ T cells originate from cross-reactive CMV-specific T cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing T cell clones reactive to both SARS-CoV-2 spike and CMV pp65 peptides.

claim: Spike-specific CD8+ T cells recognize SARS-CoV-2 spike peptide FVSNGTHWF (FVS) presented by HLA-B*35:01.
source: Spike-specific CD8+ T cells recognize SARS-CoV-2 spike peptide FVSNGTHWF (FVS) and dissimilar CMV pp65 peptide IPSINVHHY (IPS) presented by HLA-B*35:01.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from peptide library screening and functional assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: Spike-specific CD8+ T cells recognize CMV pp65 peptide IPSINVHHY (IPS) presented by HLA-B*35:01.
source: Spike-specific CD8+ T cells recognize SARS-CoV-2 spike peptide FVSNGTHWF (FVS) and dissimilar CMV pp65 peptide IPSINVHHY (IPS) presented by HLA-B*35:01.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from CPL assays and functional assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: Dual IPS/FVS-reactive CD8+ T cells were found in multiple donors.
source: These dual IPS/FVS-reactive CD8+ T cells were found in multiple donors as well as severe COVID-19 patients and shared a common T cell receptor (TCR), illustrating that IPS/FVS-cross-reactivity is caused by a public TCR.
evidence: This is supported by tetramer staining data from multiple donors shown in Figure 4.

claim: Dual IPS/FVS-reactive CD8+ T cells were found in severe COVID-19 patients.
source: These dual IPS/FVS-reactive CD8+ T cells were found in multiple donors as well as severe COVID-19 patients and shared a common T cell receptor (TCR), illustrating that IPS/FVS-cross-reactivity is caused by a public TCR.
evidence: This is supported by tetramer staining data from COVID-19 patients shown in Figure 6.

claim: IPS/FVS-reactive CD8+ T cells share a common T cell receptor (TCR).
source: These dual IPS/FVS-reactive CD8+ T cells were found in multiple donors as well as severe COVID-19 patients and shared a common T cell receptor (TCR), illustrating that IPS/FVS-cross-reactivity is caused by a public TCR.
evidence: This is supported by TCR sequencing data showing identical CDR3 sequences across multiple donors in Figure 5.

claim: IPS/FVS-cross-reactivity is caused by a public TCR.
source: These dual IPS/FVS-reactive CD8+ T cells were found in multiple donors as well as severe COVID-19 patients and shared a common T cell receptor (TCR), illustrating that IPS/FVS-cross-reactivity is caused by a public TCR.
evidence: This is supported by TCR sequencing data showing identical CDR3 sequences across multiple donors in Figure 5.

claim: CMV-specific T cells cross-react with SARS-CoV-2, despite low sequence homology between the two viruses.
source: In conclusion, CMV-specific T cells cross-react with SARS-CoV-2, despite low sequence homology between the two viruses, and may contribute to the pre-existing immunity against SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing cross-reactivity between dissimilar peptides IPS and FVS.

claim: CMV-specific T cells may contribute to the pre-existing immunity against SARS-CoV-2.
source: In conclusion, CMV-specific T cells cross-react with SARS-CoV-2, despite low sequence homology between the two viruses, and may contribute to the pre-existing immunity against SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the detection of cross-reactive T cells in unexposed donors.

claim: CD4+ and CD8+ T cells are important components of the adaptive immune system during SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: CD4+ and CD8+ T cells are important components of the adaptive immune system as CD4+ T cells promote antibody production by B cells and help cytotoxic CD8+ T cells to mediate cytotoxic lysis of SARS-CoV-2 infected cells (Sette and Crotty, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sette and Crotty, 2021.

claim: An effective T cell response has been associated with less severe COVID-19.
source: Whilst immunity is commonly measured solely based on antibody titers, research into coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pathophysiology and vaccination effectiveness has associated an effective T cell response with less severe COVID-19 (Bange et al., 2021; Bertoletti et al., 2021; Liao et al., 2020; Rydyznski Moderbacher et al., 2020; Sekine et al., 2020; Sette and Crotty, 2021; Tan et al., 2021a).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: SARS-CoV-2-specific T cell responses have been shown to be present in most individuals 6 months after infection or vaccination.
source: Additionally, SARS-CoV-2-specific T cell responses have been shown to be present in most individuals 6 months after infection or vaccination and remain largely unaffected by emerging variants of concern, illustrating their importance in generating durable immune responses (Chiuppesi et al., 2022; Choi et al., 2022; Gao et al., 2022; GeurtsvanKessel et al., 2022; Jung et al., 2022; Keeton et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2022; Redd et al., 2022; Tarke et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: SARS-CoV-2-specific T cell responses remain largely unaffected by emerging variants of concern.
source: Additionally, SARS-CoV-2-specific T cell responses have been shown to be present in most individuals 6 months after infection or vaccination and remain largely unaffected by emerging variants of concern, illustrating their importance in generating durable immune responses (Chiuppesi et al., 2022; Choi et al., 2022; Gao et al., 2022; GeurtsvanKessel et al., 2022; Jung et al., 2022; Keeton et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2022; Redd et al., 2022; Tarke et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells have been identified in unexposed individuals.
source: Besides de novo SARS-CoV-2-specific T cell responses in infected individuals, SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells have also been identified in unexposed individuals (Grifoni et al., 2020; Le Bert et al., 2020; Mateus et al., 2020; Nelde et al., 2021; Weiskopf et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Most research on pre-existing SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells has focused on cross-reactive T cells potentially primed by other human coronaviruses (HCoVs).
source: For this reason, most research has focused on cross-reactive T cells that are potentially primed by other human coronaviruses (HCoVs) since they share around 30% amino acid sequence homology with SARS-CoV-2 (Bacher et al., 2020; Braun et al., 2020; Johansson et al., 2021; Kundu et al., 2022; Le Bert et al., 2020; Loyal et al., 2021; Mateus et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Other human coronaviruses share around 30% amino acid sequence homology with SARS-CoV-2.
source: For this reason, most research has focused on cross-reactive T cells that are potentially primed by other human coronaviruses (HCoVs) since they share around 30% amino acid sequence homology with SARS-CoV-2 (Bacher et al., 2020; Braun et al., 2020; Johansson et al., 2021; Kundu et al., 2022; Le Bert et al., 2020; Loyal et al., 2021; Mateus et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: It has been postulated that SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells in unexposed individuals could be primed by non-HCoVs.
source: However, it has been postulated that SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells in unexposed individuals could also conceivably be primed by other, non-HCoVs (Le Bert et al., 2020; Peng et al., 2020; Stervbo et al., 2020; Tan et al., 2021b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Cross-reactivity between two epitopes with relatively low sequence homology has been demonstrated in previous studies.
source: Furthermore, previous studies, although limited, have demonstrated the occurrence of cross-reactivity between two epitopes with relatively low sequence homology (Bijen et al., 2018; Cameron et al., 2013; Clute et al., 2005; Cornberg et al., 2010; Riley et al., 2018; Su and Davis, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Heterologous immunity with low sequence homology is poorly understood.
source: This form of heterologous immunity is poorly understood, and therefore, predicting such cross-reactivity remains a challenge (Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2020.

claim: Pre-pandemic SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells are present in a relatively high proportion of the population, independent of geographical location.
source: Pre-pandemic SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells are reportedly present in a relatively high proportion of the population, independent of geographical location, indicating that a highly prevalent pathogen could be the initial trigger of these cross-reactive T cells (Braun et al., 2020; Grifoni et al., 2020; Le Bert et al., 2020; Mateus et al., 2020; Meckiff et al., 2020; Nelde et al., 2021; Sekine et al., 2020; Weiskopf et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: CMV is a highly prevalent pathogen that usually induces high T cell frequencies.
source: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a highly prevalent pathogen and usually induces high T cell frequencies, making CMV a potential trigger for cross-reactive SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells (Sylwester et al., 2005; Zuhair et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Sylwester et al., 2005 and Zuhair et al., 2019.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 cross-reactive CD8+ T cells were increased in CMV-seropositive donors.
source: This is supported by the finding that SARS-CoV-2 cross-reactive CD8+ T cells were increased in CMV-seropositive (CMV+) donors and that previous CMV infection has been associated with severe COVID-19 (Alanio et al., 2022; Jo et al., 2021; Weber et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Previous CMV infection has been associated with severe COVID-19.
source: This is supported by the finding that SARS-CoV-2 cross-reactive CD8+ T cells were increased in CMV-seropositive (CMV+) donors and that previous CMV infection has been associated with severe COVID-19 (Alanio et al., 2022; Jo et al., 2021; Weber et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: All CMV+ donors displayed a CD4+ and/or CD8+ T cell response upon stimulation with pp65.
source: As expected, all CMV+ donors displayed a CD4+ and/or CD8+ T cell response upon stimulation with pp65 (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: Six donors in the CMV+ group displayed a CD4+ T cell response against the membrane peptide pool which was not observed in the CMV− group.
source: However, six donors in the CMV+ group displayed a CD4+ T cell response against the membrane peptide pool which was not observed in the CMV− group (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: CD4+ T cell response against the membrane pool was accompanied by a CD4+ T cell response against pp65.
source: Furthermore, CD4+ T cell response against the membrane pool was accompanied by a CD4+ T cell response against pp65 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: CD8+ T cell responses were detected against spike peptides in two CMV+ donors which were not detected in CMV− donors.
source: In addition, CD8+ T cell responses were detected against spike peptides in two CMV+ donors which were not detected in CMV− donors (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Donors with a high CD8+ T cell response against SARS-CoV-2 spike peptides additionally displayed strong reactivity against pp65.
source: Interestingly, donors with a high CD8+ T cell response against SARS-CoV-2 spike peptides additionally displayed strong reactivity against pp65 (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: 20 out of 27 screened T cell clones produced IFN-γ when stimulated with membrane peptide pool.
source: After clonal expansion, 20 out of 27 screened T cell clones produced IFN-γ when stimulated with membrane peptide pool compared to no peptide stimulation (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as experimental data, though the data is not shown.

claim: T cell clones 4UGT5, 4UGT8, and 4UGT17 all express different TCRs.
source: T cell clones 4UGT5, 4UGT8, and 4UGT17, all three expressing a different TCR, were used for further experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by TCR sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The CD4+ T cell clones were reactive against both SARS-CoV-2 membrane antigen and CMV pp65 when loaded on HLA-matched EBV-LCLs.
source: As hypothesized, the T cell clones were reactive against both SARS-CoV-2 membrane antigen and CMV pp65 when loaded on HLA-matched EBV-lymphoblastoid cell lines (EBV-LCLs; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: IFN-γ production by the CD4+ T cell clones was significantly increased when stimulated with pp65 peptides compared to membrane peptides.
source: Interestingly, IFN-γ production by the T cell clones was significantly increased when stimulated with pp65 peptides compared to membrane peptides, indicating higher avidity for CMV compared to SARS-CoV-2 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: T cell clone 4UGT8 recognizes pp65 peptide AGILARNLVPM.
source: To identify which peptide in pp65 is recognized, reactivity of T cell clone 4UGT8 against a pp65 library was measured which resulted in recognition of three sub pools which contained peptide AGILARNLVPM (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–C.

claim: T cell clone 4UGT8 recognized both peptide pools and the AGI peptide only when presented in HLA-DRB3*02:02.
source: T cell clone 4UGT8 recognized both peptide pools and the AGI peptide only when presented in HLA-DRB3*02:02 (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: 23 out of 28 CD8+ T cell clones produced IFN-γ upon spike peptide pool stimulation.
source: The isolated CD8+ T cell clones were screened for their reactivity with SARS-CoV-2 spike which showed that 23 out of the 28 T cell clones produced IFN-γ upon spike peptide pool stimulation (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as experimental data, though the data is not shown.

claim: All 23 spike-reactive CD8+ T cell clones expressed the same TCR.
source: TCR sequencing revealed that all 23T cell clones expressed the same TCR (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by TCR sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: T cell clone 8UTT6 recognized spike as well as pp65 peptide pool presented by K562 cells transduced with HLA-B*35:01.
source: The results confirmed that T cell clone 8UTT6 recognized spike as well as pp65 peptide pool presented by K562 cells transduced with HLA-B*35:01 but not transduced with HLA-A*11:01 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: T cell clone 8UTT6 did not recognize spike or pp65 peptide pools when presented by K562 cells transduced with HLA-A*11:01.
source: The results confirmed that T cell clone 8UTT6 recognized spike as well as pp65 peptide pool presented by K562 cells transduced with HLA-B*35:01 but not transduced with HLA-A*11:01 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The FVS and IPS peptides were recognized by clone 8UTT6.
source: The FVS and IPS peptides were indeed recognized by clone 8UTT6 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The IPS peptide was recognized with higher avidity compared to the FVS peptide by clone 8UTT6.
source: Importantly, the IPS peptide was recognized with higher avidity compared to the FVS peptide by clone 8UTT6 (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by peptide titration data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The same TCRβ chain was already described and demonstrated to be specific for IPS in HLA-B*35:01.
source: Supporting these findings, the same TCRβ chain was already described and demonstrated to be specific for IPS in HLA-B*35:01 (Klarenbeek et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Klarenbeek et al., 2012.

claim: The two peptides IPS and FVS share two residues (P3-S and P7-H).
source: The two peptides share two residues (P3-S and P7-H) and have two similar residues (P6-T/V and P9-F/Y) based on similar biochemical properties and size.
evidence: This is based on structural modeling analysis described in the text.

claim: The two peptides IPS and FVS have two similar residues (P6-T/V and P9-F/Y) based on similar biochemical properties and size.
source: The two peptides share two residues (P3-S and P7-H) and have two similar residues (P6-T/V and P9-F/Y) based on similar biochemical properties and size.
evidence: This is based on structural modeling analysis described in the text.

claim: Not all T cells that bound to B*35/IPS-tetramer were able to bind to the B*35/FVS-tetramer.
source: Tetramer staining of PBMCs from donor UTT demonstrated that not all T cells that bound to B*35/IPS-tetramer were able to bind to the B*35/FVS-tetramer as well.
evidence: This is supported by tetramer staining data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: All T cells that bound to B*35/FVS-tetramer were also binding to the B*35/IPS-tetramer.
source: However, all T cells that bound to B*35/FVS-tetramer were also binding to the B*35/IPS-tetramer (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by tetramer staining data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: IPS/FVS cross-reactivity is dictated by specific TCR sequences.
source: This observation indicates that IPS/FVS cross-reactivity is dictated by specific TCR sequences which were further supported by the lack of binding to B*35/FVS-tetramer by an IPS-specific T cell clone with a different TCR (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by tetramer staining data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Nearly all CMV+ donors had IPS-specific T cells with frequencies above background level.
source: Screening of SARS-CoV-2-unexposed, CMV+, and HLA-B*35(:01) donors (N=37) showed that nearly all CMV+ donors had IPS-specific T cells with frequencies above background level, and interestingly, three of the analyzed donors (UTT, UBV, and SFW) presented with clearly detectable IPS/FVS-specific T cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by tetramer staining data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Three donors (UTT, UBV, and SFW) presented with clearly detectable IPS/FVS-specific T cells.
source: Screening of SARS-CoV-2-unexposed, CMV+, and HLA-B*35(:01) donors (N=37) showed that nearly all CMV+ donors had IPS-specific T cells with frequencies above background level, and interestingly, three of the analyzed donors (UTT, UBV, and SFW) presented with clearly detectable IPS/FVS-specific T cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by tetramer staining data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: IPS/FVS-specific T cells displayed an effector memory phenotype (CCR7−CD45RA−).
source: Furthermore, IPS/FVS-specific T cells displayed an effector memory phenotype (CCR7−CD45RA−), confirming a memory repertoire origin and, interestingly, a less differentiated phenotype compared to IPS-specific T cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: IPS/FVS-specific T cells have a less differentiated phenotype compared to IPS-specific T cells.
source: Furthermore, IPS/FVS-specific T cells displayed an effector memory phenotype (CCR7−CD45RA−), confirming a memory repertoire origin and, interestingly, a less differentiated phenotype compared to IPS-specific T cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: B*35/FVS-isolated T cells from all donors displayed amino acid identical dominant CDR3 of the α-chain, CAGNQGGKLIF.
source: Interestingly, B*35/FVS-isolated T cells from all donors displayed amino acid identical dominant complementary-determining region 3 (CDR3) of the α-chain, CAGNQGGKLIF (CDR3αCAGNQG), and β-chain, CASSLALDEQFF (CDR3βCASSLA; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by TCR sequencing data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: B*35/FVS-isolated T cells from all donors displayed amino acid identical dominant CDR3 of the β-chain, CASSLALDEQFF.
source: Interestingly, B*35/FVS-isolated T cells from all donors displayed amino acid identical dominant complementary-determining region 3 (CDR3) of the α-chain, CAGNQGGKLIF (CDR3αCAGNQG), and β-chain, CASSLALDEQFF (CDR3βCASSLA; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by TCR sequencing data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Both CDR3αCAGNQG and CDR3βCASSLA were identified in all samples sorted on B*35/IPS-tetramer binding and shown to be among the most dominant TCRs.
source: Both CDR3αCAGNQG and CDR3βCASSLA were identified in all samples and shown to be among the most dominant TCRs.
evidence: This is supported by TCR sequencing data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The public TCR was present in donor JZX which showed IPS/FVS-tetramer+ T cells below background level.
source: Remarkably, this was also observed in donor JZX which showed IPS/FVS-tetramer+ T cells below background level, indicating that in more than 3 out of 37 donors, this public TCR is present. (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by TCR sequencing data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In more than 3 out of 37 donors, the public TCR is present.
source: Remarkably, this was also observed in donor JZX which showed IPS/FVS-tetramer+ T cells below background level, indicating that in more than 3 out of 37 donors, this public TCR is present. (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the detection of the public TCR in donor JZX.

claim: IPS/FVS-specific T cells were able to recognize endogenously processed and presented peptide.
source: Firstly, the reactivity of IPS/FVS-specific T cells against K562 transduced with the spike gene was measured which showed that the T cells were able to recognize endogenously processed and presented peptide (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 spike-specific CD8+ T cells from a SARS-CoV-2 vaccinated donor were able to reduce intracellular SARS-CoV-2 RNA copies at both 0.05 and 0.5 MOI 24 hr post infection.
source: SARS-CoV-2 spike-specific CD8+ T cells from a SARS-CoV-2 vaccinated donor were able to reduce intracellular SARS-CoV-2 RNA copies at both 0.05 and 0.5 multiplicity of infection (MOI) 24 hr post infection (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B–C.

claim: IPS/FVS-specific CD8+ T cells were able to reduce SARS-CoV-2 intracellular RNA copies in Calu-3 cells infected with 0.05 MOI.
source: Interestingly, IPS/FVS-specific CD8+ T cells were able to reduce SARS-CoV-2 intracellular RNA copies in Calu-3 cells infected with 0.05 MOI (MOI Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Incubating IPS/FVS-specific CD8+ T cells with 0.5 MOI resulted in no difference in RNA copies compared to the no T cell control.
source: Incubating with 10-fold more virus (0.5 MOI) resulted in no difference in RNA copies compared to the no T cell control (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: IPS/FVS-cross-reactive T cells were detected in two out of two CMV+ HLA-B*35:01+ patients suffering from severe COVID-19.
source: Interestingly, IPS/FVS-cross-reactive T cells were detected in two out of two CMV+ HLA-B*35:01+ patients suffering from severe COVID-19, whereas the cross-reactive T cells were detected in 3 out of 37 healthy CMV+ HLA-B*35:01+ donors (Figures 4C and 6E).
evidence: This is supported by tetramer staining data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The expression of CD38 and HLA-DR on IPS/FVS-specific T cells was lower compared to the SARS-CoV-2-specific CD8+ T cells.
source: The expression of CD38 and HLA-DR was lower compared to the SARS-CoV-2-specific CD8+ T cells and not considerably increased compared to IPS-specific T cells that were not cross-reactive with FVS (Figure 6D–E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6D–E.

claim: The expression of CD38 and HLA-DR on IPS/FVS-specific T cells was not considerably increased compared to IPS-specific T cells that were not cross-reactive with FVS.
source: The expression of CD38 and HLA-DR was lower compared to the SARS-CoV-2-specific CD8+ T cells and not considerably increased compared to IPS-specific T cells that were not cross-reactive with FVS (Figure 6D–E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6D–E.

claim: IPS/FVS-specific CD8+ T cells recognize SARS-CoV-2-infected cells and are able to limit SARS-CoV-2 replication at low virus titers.
source: These results indicate that IPS/FVS-specific CD8+ T cells recognize SARS-CoV-2-infected cells and are able to limit SARS-CoV-2 replication at low virus titers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from the infection assays.

claim: IPS/FVS-specific T cells did not show an activated phenotype during acute severe SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: However, IPS/FVS-specific T cells did not show an activated phenotype during acute severe SARS-CoV-2 infection.
evidence: This is based on the flow cytometry data showing low expression of activation markers.

claim: This is the first study to identify CMV-specific T cells that are cross reactive with SARS-CoV-2.
source: To our knowledge this is the first study to identify CMV-specific T cells that are cross reactive with SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: The cross-reactive CD4+ T cells recognized CMV pp65 epitope AGILARNLVPM in HLA-DRB3*02:02.
source: The cross-reactive CD4+ T cells recognized CMV pp65 epitope AGILARNLVPM in HLA-DRB3*02:02 and were able to cross react with an as of yet unidentified, SARS-CoV-2 membrane epitope in HLA-DRB3*02:02 (Weber et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from co-culture assays.

claim: The cross-reactive CD4+ T cells were able to cross react with an as of yet unidentified, SARS-CoV-2 membrane epitope in HLA-DRB3*02:02.
source: The cross-reactive CD4+ T cells recognized CMV pp65 epitope AGILARNLVPM in HLA-DRB3*02:02 and were able to cross react with an as of yet unidentified, SARS-CoV-2 membrane epitope in HLA-DRB3*02:02 (Weber et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from co-culture assays.

claim: Previous studies have reported the presence of membrane-specific CD4+ T cell responses in SARS-CoV-2-unexposed donors utilizing the same commercially available membrane peptide pool.
source: Previous studies have reported the presence of membrane-specific CD4+ T cell responses in SARS-CoV-2-unexposed donors utilizing the same commercially available membrane peptide pool, yet these studies did not aim to identify the peptide-HLA restriction (Bacher et al., 2020; Sekine et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Bacher et al., 2020 and Sekine et al., 2020.

claim: AGI-specific CD4+ T cells have been described to be cross reactive toward SARS-CoV-2 spike.
source: AGI-specific CD4+ T cells have been described to be cross reactive toward SARS-CoV-2 spike which is in contrast to our finding (Weber et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Weber et al., 2022.

claim: The cross-reactive CD8+ T cells recognize the CMV epitope IPSINVHHY and SARS-CoV-2 epitope FVSNGTHWF presented in HLA-B*35:01.
source: The cross-reactive CD8+ T cells recognize the CMV epitope IPSINVHHY and SARS-CoV-2 epitope FVSNGTHWF presented in HLA-B*35:01.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from peptide identification assays.

claim: IPS/FVS-specific T cells were possibly detected previously but never further investigated or characterized.
source: IPS/FVS-specific T cells were possibly detected previously but never further investigated or characterized (Shomuradova et al., 2020; Tarke et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Shomuradova et al., 2020 and Tarke et al., 2021.

claim: Both cross-reactive CD4+ and CD8+ T cells displayed a higher avidity for the CMV epitope compared to the epitope derived from SARS-CoV-2.
source: Both cross-reactive CD4+ and CD8+ T cells displayed a higher avidity for the CMV epitope compared to the epitope derived from SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is supported by peptide titration data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Other studies have reported an equal or even higher avidity for the SARS-CoV-2 epitope compared to the epitopes derived from the HCoV for which the T cells were hypothesized to be primed against.
source: In contrast, other studies have reported an equal or even higher avidity for the SARS-CoV-2 epitope compared to the epitopes derived from the HCoV for which the T cells were hypothesized to be primed against (Braun et al., 2020; Johansson et al., 2021; Lineburg et al., 2021; Mateus et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Repeated exposure results in the selection of high avidity T cell clonotypes which are able to clear viral infection and protect against reinfection.
source: This appears to be contradictive since it has been shown that repeated exposure results in the selection of high avidity T cell clonotypes which are able to clear viral infection and protect against reinfection (Abdel-Hakeem et al., 2017; Hombrink et al., 2013; Price et al., 2005; Schober et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Cross-reactive T cells would most likely display a higher avidity for the source pathogen compared to the avidity for SARS-CoV-2.
source: Cross-reactive T cells would therefore most likely display a higher avidity for the source pathogen compared to the avidity for SARS-CoV-2, as reported in this study.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about T cell avidity and repeated exposure.

claim: The contribution of other HCoVs as initial primers of the T cell response may have been over-estimated due to experimental design.
source: Taken together, whereas cross-reactive T cells recognizing SARS-CoV-2 have been primarily described to be derived from other HCoVs, the contribution of these other HCoVs as initial primers of the T cell response may have been over-estimated due to experimental design.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the discussion of avidity and experimental design issues.

claim: Further studies are required to identify other potential sources of cross reactivity with low sequence homology yet high prevalences such as CMV, EBV, influenza, or non-viral pathogens.
source: Further studies are required to identify other potential sources of cross reactivity with low sequence homology yet high prevalences such as CMV, EBV, influenza, or non-viral pathogens.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research.

claim: Ex vivo detected heterologous CD8+ T cell immunity against two pathogens caused by dissimilar epitopes presented in the same HLA is rarely reported.
source: Ex vivo detected heterologous CD8+ T cell immunity against two pathogens caused by dissimilar epitopes presented in the same HLA is rarely reported (Clute et al., 2005; Cornberg et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Clute et al., 2005 and Cornberg et al., 2010.

claim: Heterologous immunity can be caused by the expression of a dual TCR.
source: Heterologous immunity can be caused by the expression of a dual TCR which means that two TCR α- or β-chains are expressed simultaneously, resulting in two distinctive TCRs within one T cell (Cusick et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Cusick et al., 2012.

claim: A single TCR was identified in cross-reactive T cells, excluding the dual TCR hypothesis.
source: However, here, we identified a single TCR in cross-reactive T cells excluding this hypothesis.
evidence: This is supported by TCR sequencing data.

claim: Recognition of two distinct epitopes by a single TCR can be explained by shape similarity once the peptides are bound to the HLA molecule.
source: Recognition of two distinct epitopes by a single TCR can be explained by shape similarity once the peptides are bound to the HLA molecule, and this shape similarity, or molecular mimicry can underpin T cell cross reactivity (Macdonald et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Macdonald et al., 2009.

claim: Similarity between the IPS and FVS peptides in backbone conformation and the C-terminal part might underpin the T cell cross reactivity observed.
source: Here, similarity between the IPS and FVS peptides in backbone conformation and the C-terminal part might underpin the T cell cross reactivity observed, as the majority of TCR docks preferentially toward the C-terminal of the peptide (Szeto et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on structural modeling and supported by a citation to Szeto et al., 2020.

claim: The majority of TCR docks preferentially toward the C-terminal of the peptide.
source: Here, similarity between the IPS and FVS peptides in backbone conformation and the C-terminal part might underpin the T cell cross reactivity observed, as the majority of TCR docks preferentially toward the C-terminal of the peptide (Szeto et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Szeto et al., 2020.

claim: The presence of cross-reactive memory T cells in circulation may be an advantage during initial SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: The presence of these cross-reactive memory T cells in circulation may be an advantage during initial SARS-CoV-2 infection as rapid T cell responses were associated with less severe COVID-19 (Loyal et al., 2021; Sette and Crotty, 2021; Tan et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Rapid T cell responses were associated with less severe COVID-19.
source: The presence of these cross-reactive memory T cells in circulation may be an advantage during initial SARS-CoV-2 infection as rapid T cell responses were associated with less severe COVID-19 (Loyal et al., 2021; Sette and Crotty, 2021; Tan et al., 2021a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The cross-reactive CD8+ T cells were less efficient compared to SARS-CoV-2-specific, vaccination-primed T cells in limiting viral spread in vitro.
source: However, the cross-reactive CD8+ T cells were less efficient compared to SARS-CoV-2-specific, vaccination-primed T cells in limiting viral spread in vitro which can be explained by the reduced avidity of the cross-reactive T cells for the spike protein compared to CMV.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the infection assays shown in Figure 6.

claim: IPS/FVS-specific CD8+ T cells might be able to reduce SARS-CoV-2 spread at initial infection but likely do not play a significant role in the pathogenesis of severe COVID-19.
source: These observations together indicate that IPS/FVS-specific CD8+ T cells might be able to reduce SARS-CoV-2 spread at initial infection but likely do not play a significant role in the pathogenesis of severe COVID-19.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the activation state and functional data.

claim: The study focused on circulating T cells, and it cannot be excluded that cross-reactive CD8+ T cells present in lung tissue displayed an activated phenotype.
source: One limitation is that our study focused on circulating T cells, and we cannot exclude the possibility that cross-reactive CD8+ T cells present in lung tissue did display an activated phenotype.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Additional studies using larger cohorts are required to fully elucidate the potential role of cross-reactive CD8+ T cells in disease.
source: In summary, additional studies using larger cohorts are required to fully elucidate the potential role of cross-reactive CD8+ T cells in disease.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research.

claim: Pre-pandemic SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells can derive from non-homologous pathogens such as CMV.
source: In conclusion, pre-pandemic SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells can derive from non-homologous pathogens such as CMV.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: This expands the potential origin of pre-pandemic SARS-CoV-2-specific CD4+ and CD8+ T cell beyond other HCoVs.
source: This expands the potential origin of these pre-pandemic SARS-CoV-2-specific CD4+ and CD8+ T cell beyond other HCoVs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The cross-reactive CD8+ T cells were reactive toward dissimilar epitopes, and this cross reactivity was caused by a public TCR.
source: The cross-reactive CD8+ T cells were reactive toward dissimilar epitopes, and this cross reactivity was caused by a public TCR, which has been rarely observed so far.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Cross-reactivity caused by a public TCR toward dissimilar epitopes has been rarely observed.
source: The cross-reactive CD8+ T cells were reactive toward dissimilar epitopes, and this cross reactivity was caused by a public TCR, which has been rarely observed so far.
evidence: This is a claim about the rarity of this phenomenon in the literature.

claim: The data points toward a role of the cross-reactive T cells in reducing SARS-CoV-2 viral load in the early stages of infection, prior to priming of SARS-CoV-2 specific T cells.
source: Our data points toward a role of the cross-reactive T cells in reducing SARS-CoV-2 viral load in the early stages of infection, prior to priming of SARS-CoV-2 specific T cells.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the functional data from the infection assays.

claim: These results aid in further understanding heterologous T cell immunity beyond common cold coronaviruses.
source: Altogether, these results aid in further understanding heterologous T cell immunity beyond common cold coronaviruses and facilitate the investigation into the potential role of cross-reactive T cells in COVID-19.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the significance of the study.

claim: Memory SARS-CoV-2-specific CD4+ T cells were characterized as CD154+CD137+.
source: Memory SARS-CoV-2-specific CD4+ T cells were characterized as CD154+CD137+, and memory SARS-CoV-2-specific CD8+ T cells were identified based on expression of CD137 and IFN-γ (Figure 1A–B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a methodological description supported by flow cytometry data.

claim: Memory SARS-CoV-2-specific CD8+ T cells were identified based on expression of CD137 and IFN-γ.
source: Memory SARS-CoV-2-specific CD4+ T cells were characterized as CD154+CD137+, and memory SARS-CoV-2-specific CD8+ T cells were identified based on expression of CD137 and IFN-γ (Figure 1A–B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a methodological description supported by flow cytometry data.

claim: The FVS peptide might adopt a similar backbone conformation compared to the IPS peptide.
source: Overall, the FVS peptide might adopt a similar backbone conformation compared to the IPS peptide, which would place in both peptides a small hydrophobic residue at position 6 (P6-T/V), a histidine at position 7, and a residue with a large side-chain at position 8 (P8-W/H).
evidence: This is based on structural modeling analysis.

claim: The primary anchor in the FVS peptide is P2-V and P9-F.
source: The primary anchor in the FVS peptide is P2-V and P9-F, both within the favored residues at those positions for HLA-B35-restricted peptide (Escobar et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on structural modeling and supported by a citation to Escobar et al., 2008.

claim: The lack of secondary anchor residue at position 5 in the FVS peptide (P5-N/G) might change the conformation of the central part of the peptide.
source: The lack of secondary anchor residue at position 5 in the FVS peptide (P5-N/G) might change the conformation of the central part of the peptide that could be similar to the one observed in the spike-derived peptide IPF (S896-904) in complex with HLA-B*35:01 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Nguyen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on structural modeling and supported by a citation to Nguyen et al., 2021.

claim: Residue substitutions from the IPS to FVS peptide were possible without major steric clashes with the HLA or peptide residues.
source: Residue substitutions from the IPS to FVS peptide were possible without major steric clashes with the HLA or peptide residues.
evidence: This is based on structural modeling analysis.

claim: CD38 and HLA-DR are highly expressed on SARS-CoV-2-specific CD8+ T cells during severe COVID-19.
source: The activation state was measured by expression of activation markers CD38 and HLA-DR as these markers are highly expressed on SARS-CoV-2-specific CD8+ T cells during severe COVID-19 (Figure 6D; Sekine et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sekine et al., 2020.

claim: The prevalence of IPS/FVS-specific T cells in severe COVID-19 patients (2 out of 2) was higher than in healthy donors (3 out of 37).
source: Interestingly, IPS/FVS-cross-reactive T cells were detected in two out of two CMV+ HLA-B*35:01+ patients suffering from severe COVID-19, whereas the cross-reactive T cells were detected in 3 out of 37 healthy CMV+ HLA-B*35:01+ donors (Figures 4C and 6E).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the prevalence data between patient and donor cohorts.
